--- title: "Introduction to R" subtitle: "PSYC 6019-A01 / PSYC 6022-A01 \n 2026-08-28 | Lab 1" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss preview-links: true # theme: "../../../../../../../../OneDrive - Georgia Institute of Technology/Courses/GTA/PSYC 6019/PSYC6019-2026/gt-theme" execute: echo: true freeze: auto --- ## Outline - Introductions! - Lab Syllabus - What is R? - RStudio Layout - R Basics - Quarto Basics ## Instructor Introduction Hi! I'm Jess Helmer. I'm a third-year PhD student in Quantitative Psychology. My research focuses on the measurement and modeling of psychological data. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: subpoint ○ Email: [jhelmer3\@gatech.edu](mailto:jhelmer3\@gatech.edu) ::: ::: subpoint ○ Office: J.S. Coon Rm 240 ::: ::: subpoint ○ Office Hours: Fridays, 1–2pm, my office / Zoom ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ Or by appointment ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ![](../media/lab_01/lily.jpg){width=250} ![](../media/lab_01/sheba.jpg){width=250} ::: :::: ## What You Can Expect From Me I am available as a resource! Please feel free to reach out / email anytime if you need help, have questions about the lab, or have any suggestions or feedback for the class. I encourage helping each other / collaboration during the lab. While working on assignments, I will try to answer everyone's questions as soon as I can, but if someone near you is confused and you can help, feel free to discuss. ## Student Introductions - Name - Program - Coding Experience? R? - Anything else! ## Lab Assignments Students are expected to attend and participate in all scheduled labs. We will have a lab lecture and activity each week (barring institute holidays). Students are expected to work on the activity during the scheduled lab time. Lab assignments are due on Canvas at 11:59pm the same day they are distributed. We will not be able to accept late lab assignments! Assignment distributed after lecture (with plenty of time to complete!) ## Lab Assignments **Always** offer a few words of explanation for questions in the assignment. ::: subpoint ○ Output alone will not get full credit. ::: Please submit both the rendered (.html or .pdf) and the source Quarto (.qmd) file. ::: subpoint ○ Without your R code, we will not be able to give partial credit if the result is incorrect. ::: **Always** provide R output for every analysis carried out. ::: subpoint ○ If the assignment asks you to make a plot, include that plot in your submission (not just the code). ::: As long as a complete attempt is made, full credit will be given. ## Lab Project One of the best ways to learn R is to work on an independent data analysis project with real data. Opportunity to immerse yourself in the language, explore the messiness of real data, make and learn from mistakes. We can provide you with a dataset if needed, but you are strongly encouraged to find data you are particularly interested in. More details to come---will be due at the end of the semester. ## About AI AI can be a very helpful tool for learning coding! Feel free to use it to clarify concepts, troubleshoot code, or syntax explanations. However, for the assignments, your code needs to be your own. It is important to practice and gain experiencing coding independently! ## Lab Resources :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="30%"} [R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/){target="blank"} [![](../media/lab_01/r4de.jpg)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/){target="blank"} ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} [ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis (3e)](https://ggplot2-book.org/) [![](../media/lab_01/ggplot2.jpg)](https://ggplot2-book.org//) ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} [Quarto Documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/) [![](../media/lab_01/quarto.png)](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/) ::: :::: All free, open source materials for learning R ## Lab Resources (Other) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="30%"} [Introduction to Data Exploration and Analysis with R (IDEAR)](https://bookdown.org/mikemahoney218/IDEAR/) Similar content as R4DS but with a different writing style. ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} [What They Forgot to Teach You About R](https://rstats.wtf/) ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} [Happy Git with R](https://happygitwithr.com/) An excellent resource for getting started with Git and GitHub as an R user. ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Any questions on syllabus, assignments, materials? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What is R? Open source coding language, primarily used for data analysis and data science. ![](../media/lab_01/R.png){.absolute width="200" bottom=20 right=0} Coding (per the IDEAR book): ::: fragment "Giving very specific instructions to a very stupid machine." :::
::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print("Hello, World!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Hello, World!" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Why R? Because R is a programming language, you can make your own code / functions as commands, instead of just relying on existing features. R has many "packages" for statistical functions and a large, enthusiastic community of statistical programmers. R is open source: you can see the exact code that underlies the functions you use ::: subpoint ○ And if you'd like, you can modify it ::: ## What is RStudio? An interface for using and coding in R Helps keep R files and projects organized Helps "knit" together code, output, and text to create reports ## Installing R We need to download two things: [R](https://cloud.r-project.org/) and [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/#download) R is the language, RStudio is an Interactive Development Environment (IDE). We will use R through RStudio. ## RStudio Introduction Files, Plots, Packages Environment, History Console ## R Console ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 + 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 + 4 / 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment PEMDAS! ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 ^ 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 8 %% 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Vectors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(2, 4, 6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 4 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, "hello!", "Georgia Tech") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "hello!" "Georgia Tech" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment `c()` function - Stands for "combine" ::: ## Data Types ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, 2, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, "hello!", "Georgia Tech") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "hello!" "Georgia Tech" ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Quotes around `1` in the first vector, not in the second ::: ::: fragment Vectors can only hold one type of data! - Numeric - Character ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, 2, 3) / 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3333333 0.6666667 1.0000000 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, "hello!", "Georgia Tech") / 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `c(1, "hello!", "Georgia Tech") / 3`: ! non-numeric argument to binary operator ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment Error because we cannot divide characters ::: ::: :::: ## Variable Assignment In R, we can assign objects (including functions) to some variable with the *assignment operator* `<-`. You can also print objects by just running their name. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # assign variable a the value 1 a <- 1 # print a a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Variable Assignment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c(1, 2, 3) a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c("Hello, world!") a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Hello, world!" ``` ::: ::: Every time we reassign a value to `a`, it holds that new value Overwrites previous value! ## Variable Assignment Overwriting can mess stuff up! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../media/lab_01/goback.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fragment Generally, we want to avoid overwriting these "[reserved words](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Reserved.html)" or names of key functions. ::: ::: fragment But, how can we fix things if we do? ::: ::: :::: ## Clearing Environment and Restarting R Clearing your environment and restarting R frequently helps you reset :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### How to Clear Your Environment 1) Button ![](../media/lab_01/envclear.png) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### How to Restart R 1) Manually: ::: subpoint ○ Session \> Restart R. ::: 2) Shortcut: ::: subpoint ○ Use the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + F10 (Windows) or Cmd + Shift + F10. ::: ::: :::: ## Clearing Environment and Restarting R :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} I strongly (!!) suggest you change these default RStudio settings in order to always start R with a blank slate. Tools > Global Options ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../media/lab_01/blank-slate-settings_wtf-book.png) ::: :::: ::: footer [What They Forgot to Teach You About R](https://rstats.wtf/source-and-blank-slates#always-start-r-with-a-blank-slate) ::: ## Variables in Statistics: Numeric vs. Categorical ### Numeric ::: subpoint ○ Quantitative ::: ::: subpoint ○ Values describing a measurable quantity as a number ::: ::: subpoint ○ “How many” or “how much” ::: ### Categorical ::: subpoint ○ Distinguish distinct elements or entities ::: ::: subpoint ○ Name, gender, ethnicity... ::: ## Dataframes Table of data organized by columns Can make by hand with the `data.frame()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame( x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c("a", "b", "c"), z = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y z 1 1 a TRUE 2 2 b FALSE 3 3 c TRUE ``` ::: ::: Shift+Enter to go to new line on Console Most of the time, we import data (and don't manually type it in) In console, can press up arrow to reload last line of code ## Dataframes If you already have vector objects saved, you don't have to type them in again ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c(1, 2, 3) b <- c(2, 3, 4) c <- c(3, 4, 5) ``` :::
:::: columns ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(a = a, b = b, c = c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a b c 1 1 2 3 2 2 3 4 3 3 4 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(a, b, c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a b c 1 1 2 3 2 2 3 4 3 3 4 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.frame(A = a, b, c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` A b c 1 1 2 3 2 2 3 4 3 3 4 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## R Projects RStudio's way of helping organizing files, scripts, etc. I strongly recommend this!! ::: subpoint ○ File \> New Project ::: ::: subpoint ○ If you don't already have a folder associated with this class, "New Directory" ::: ::: subpoint ○ If you do, "Existing Directory" ::: All R Scripts under the same project share a *working directory* ○ Location of files `getwd()` tells us the location of our working directory `setwd("C:/Users/Desktop/R Example")` sets the working directory Or, `here::here()` lets us do relative directories (my favorite!) ::: subpoint ○ Just use the command at the top of the file to see where your directory is ::: ## R Scripts R script files end with .R ### How to Create an R Script File 1) Manually ::: subpoint File \> New File \> R Script ::: 2) Shortcut ::: subpoint Ctrl + Shift + N ::: ## Quarto :::: columns ::: column A way of typesetting R code into a document End in .qmd File \> New File \> Quarto Document... Input Title, Author, Date How we will complete assignments ::: ::: column ![](../media/lab_01/creating-quarto-document.png) ::: :::: ## Insert a Code Chunk How to insert an Quarto code chunk in RStudio :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} 1) Manually: ::: subpoint ○ Type ```` ```{r} ````. ::: ::: subpoint ○ Add your R code. ::: ::: subpoint ○ Close the chunk with ```` ``` ````. ::: 2) Shortcut: ::: subpoint ○ Use the shortcut Ctrl + Alt + I (Windows) or Cmd + Option + I. ::: 3) Button ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../media/lab_01/quarto-new-r-chunk.png) ::: :::: ## Run a Chunk How to run Quarto code chunks in RStudio 1) Shortcut: ::: subpoint ○ Use the shortcut Ctrl + Enter (Windows) or Ctrl + Return (Mac) ::: 2) Button ![](../media/lab_01/quarto-run-r-chunk.png) Can also select a variable and run it to see its output (helpful!) ## Revisiting Clearing Environement and Restarting R Important to ensure that your code isn't unintentionally relying on hidden objects in the environement ::: subpoint ○ E.g., you created an object, deleted the line to create it, but R still sees it there ::: When you try to render your file, it will clear, restart, and run all code Clearing your environment and restarting R frequently helps you avoid this ## Tips for Quarto! Run code often to ensure it's working Restart R frequently Rendering will combine text, syntax, results, and output into a Word, PDF, or HTML file ![](../media/lab_01/quarto-render.png) ## Adding Math Equations In Quarto, we can use LaTeX (pronounced "lah-tech" or "lay-tech") to render nice-looking math symbols and equations $$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i \qquad \quad \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{N} \qquad \quad s^2 = \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N-1} $$ For inline LaTeX (e.g., $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$), wrap the equation in single dollar signs `$a^2 = b^2 + c^2$`. For LaTeX on its own line, like above, wrap the equation in double dollar signs `$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$` $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$ ## Common LaTeX Syntax :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} | | | | |-------|---|---| | subscript | `a_i` | $a_i$ | | superscript | `a^2` | $a^2$ | Need brackets if more than one character: | | | |---|---| | `x_ij` | $x_ij$ | | `x_{ij}` | $x_{ij}$ | ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} `\` is an **escape character**: tells LaTeX to interpret the following text differently than normally | | | |---|---| | `sum` | $sum$ | | `\sum` | $\sum$ | | `\frac{a}{b}` | $\frac{a}{b}$ | | `\bar{x}` | $\bar{x}$ | | `\times` | $\times$ | ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} Greek characters | | | |---|---| | `\alpha` | $\alpha$ | | `\beta` | $\beta$ | | `\mu` | $\mu$ | | `\sigma` | $\sigma$ | ::: :::: ## LaTeX Resources An live in-browser LaTeX editor I use: [latexeditor.lagrida.com](https://latexeditor.lagrida.com/) Math symbols cheat sheet: [cmor-faculty.rice.edu/~heinken/latex/symbols.pdf](https://cmor-faculty.rice.edu/~heinken/latex/symbols.pdf) Usually pretty easy to find answers just by Googling (e.g., [me looking up the summation syntax earlier](https://duckduckgo.com/?t=ffab&q=sum+with+numbers+below+and+on+top+latex&ia=web)) and on Stack Overflow No expectation of memorizing LaTeX syntax ## Today's Dataset `iris` dataset has measurements of 150 flowers, already exists within R. :::: {.columns style="font-size:70%"} ::: {.column} `head()` function shows first elements of an object (here, rows in a dataframe). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(iris) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa 2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 setosa 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 setosa 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 setosa 5 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 setosa 6 5.4 3.9 1.7 0.4 setosa ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} `tail()` shows last few rows. Can specify how many rows you want ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tail(iris, n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 148 6.5 3.0 5.2 2.0 virginica 149 6.2 3.4 5.4 2.3 virginica 150 5.9 3.0 5.1 1.8 virginica ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: `View()` (note the capital V) will open the data in an interactive viewer. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} View(iris) ``` ::: ## Basic Descriptives `$` operator references columns within a dataframe Dataframes contain columns of variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(iris$Petal.Length) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.4 1.4 1.3 1.5 1.4 1.7 ``` ::: ::: `mean(x)` for mean, `sd(x)` for standard deviation, and `var(x)` for variance of a vector `x`. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(iris$Petal.Length) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.758 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(iris$Petal.Length) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.765298 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var(iris$Petal.Length) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.116278 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Saving Work Press Ctrl + S frequently to save your work!! Can also press the save icon in the top left ![](../media/lab_01/quarto-save.png) ## Activity 1 Objectives: - Do some basic R! - Get familiar with Quarto

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
